To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) reading on paper does not make a significant positive difference in report quality compared to reading on a laptop or tablet, (2) reading on paper may help students to read more efficiently, (3) reading on a laptop without Internet and printer access may improve report quality, but this effect is mitigated by note taking on paper, and (4) students’ preference for reading on paper is strong.

(1) reading text from a computer screen is not inferior to reading from paper; (2) multitasking while reading from a screen reduces reading efficiency; (3) reading from a computer screen without access to the Internet and a printer improves report quality, compared to reading from a computer with Internet and printer accessibility; and (4) active use of paper for taking notes while reading from a computer improves report quality in the real-world reading condition.
reading comprehension was unaffected by medium, but multitasking slowed reading.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of reading from electronic screens on the reading and writing of college students.
the impact of screen reading and multitasking conditions on reading and writing among college students.
the effect of medium of reading and opportunities to multitasking on reading and writing among college students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reading from screens is not necessarily better than reading from paper, but it is not necessarily worse either.
the medium of reading does not make a difference to the quality of the reading, as long as the reader is not distracted or multitasking.
reading on paper and computer screens are not equivalent, and reading from a computer screen is not necessarily superior to reading on paper.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reading from paper is more effective than reading from screens, and reading from screens is more effective than multitasking with screens.
the medium of reading and writing does not make a difference in quality of learning, but the conditions under which students access information and produce reports do make a difference.
the medium of reading and the opportunity for multitasking have little impact on reading and writing, but multitasking does impact efficiency of reading.
The main takeaway from our work is that

reading from paper and reading from screens are equally effective, but that reading on a screen with Internet and print access is less effective than reading from paper, and less effective than reading on a screen without Internet and print access.
reading and writing are not inherently different when done on paper versus on computer screens, but that the context of use matters.
reading on a computer screen is not necessarily detrimental to reading comprehension.
